paper_title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Picture life on planet with three suns, whose chaotic motion brings lethal heat and cold at unexpected times (Liu, 2014). Having barely survived after taking shelter day too late, one could evaluate alternative times to shelter by trying to imagine the skies and their outcomes (Sutton, 1991; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018). Yet realistic imagination needs predicting the motion of the three suns, chaotic three-body system beyond anyones control. Moreover, random variations across independently simulated skies can obscure whether sheltering earlier would actually help. This example illustrates two challenges for learning with world models in big world (Javed & Sutton, 2024). World models allow agents to evaluate alternative actions without additional environment interaction, but their usefulness depends on both predictive accuracy and the informativeness of simulated outcomes. When environmental complexity exceeds an agents modeling capacity, errors can compound across imagined trajectories (Janner et al., 2019; Assran et al., 2025). Even with an accurate model, environmental randomness can dominate simulated returns, obscuring action effects and increasing the variance of policy gradient estimates (Mao et al., 2018). In this paper, we study counterfactual world models, which take observed trajectories to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness. Looking back (Fujimoto, 2021), one might ask: given how the suns actually moved, would taking shelter day earlier have helped? Answering this question may be easier since the actual experience provides reference for predicting what would change under different decision (Roese, 1997). counterfactual model can use information about how the world unfolded and focus its predictive capacity on action-dependent changes (Buesing et al., 2018). Holding environmental randomness fixed can also help distinguish action effects from luck, reducing the variance of policy gradient estimates (Mesnard et al., 2020a). We explore two approaches to constructing counterfactual world models: (i) directly training models on paired trajectories generated under shared environmental randomness, and (ii) applying diffusion Equal contribution Equal advising Work partially done while visiting the Global AI Frontier Lab at NYU. 1Code is available at https://github.com/ToghrulAbbasov19/look-back. Preprint. Figure 1: Overview. To evaluate an action jump against the observed action stand, world model imagines the future anew (top), mixing the actions effect with luck, whereas counterfactual world model edits the observed experience, isolating it (bottom). counterfactual inference (Sanchez & Tsaftaris, 2022) to trained diffusion world models (Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025). To leverage these models for reinforcement learning, we build on RLOO (Kool et al., 2019) and introduce REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), policy gradient algorithm that generates multiple counterfactual trajectories and uses their predicted returns as baselines. Our main contributions are: We formalize counterfactual world models and two approaches to building them, covering settings with and without access to trajectory pairs generated under shared environmental randomness. We introduce RLB, policy gradient algorithm based on counterfactual return baselines, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction, and error bounds under learned models. We show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and yield better policies than ordinary world models when action effects are more predictable than environmental evolution. Our results suggest that looking back at past experience can reduce the predictive burden of learning in complex environments and help agents more precisely identify the consequences of their actions.

sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: We provide an overview of related work. An extended discussion can be found in Appendix B. World models. In model-based reinforcement learning, world models support policy learning through imagined experience (Sutton, 1991; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018). Yet, model errors arising from limited capacity can limit their utility (Janner et al., 2019), especially when modeling big world (Javed & Sutton, 2024). Prior work has addressed this challenge by directing model capacity toward predictions needed for value estimation and planning (Grimm et al., 2020; LeCun, 2022). We study complementary approach of using observed trajectories as conditioning information when predicting the consequences of alternative actions. This can simplify prediction when environmental evolution is difficult to model but action effects are comparatively simple (Buesing et al., 2018). Counterfactual reinforcement learning. Prior work has used counterfactual reasoning (Roese, 1997) to improve reinforcement learning methods. Buesing et al. (2018) show that conditioning simulations on logged experience can improve policy evaluation and search. CCA (Mesnard et al., 2020a) learns value baselines that estimate counterfactual returns in order to better distinguish action effects from environmental luck, adding an action-independence loss to encourage unbiasedness. Our approach learns imaginations using counterfactual world model to construct policy gradient baselines, harnessing benefits of counterfactuals in both model learning and credit assignment. Policy gradient baselines. Our policy gradient estimator builds on prior work on baselines, which can reduce variance without biasing the gradient under proper conditions (Greensmith et al., 2004). RLOO (Kool et al., 2019) constructs baselines from independent trajectories from the same initial state, and world models can provide these trajectories when the environment cannot be reset (Xiao et al., 2025). For environments with simulators, prior work has shown that constructing baselines from trajectories with shared randomness can further reduce variance (Schulman et al., 2015; Mao et al., 2018; Bazerghi et al., 2025) through common random number effect. Counterfactual modeling. Counterfactual modeling builds upon the causal inference framework (Pearl, 2009), with approaches including learning from paired observations with shared underlying randomness (Baradel et al., 2019) and learning diffusion model to generate counterfactuals from noise inversion of observed data (Sanchez & Tsaftaris, 2022). We adapt both to world modeling, using trajectory pairs generated under different actions and shared environmental randomness, or extending diffusion counterfactuals to action-conditioned prediction. The latter fits naturally with model-based reinforcement learning, as it builds upon diffusion world models trained on interaction data (Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025) without requiring paired counterfactual supervision.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Through our experiments, we aim to answer the following key questions: Q1. When using ground-truth counterfactuals, does RLB yield better policies than RLOO that uses ground-truth environmental simulations, as well as other policy gradient methods? Q2. Are counterfactual world models easier to learn, and do they yield better policies via RLB than ordinary world models when action effects are more predictable than environmental evolution? Q3. Can diffusion world models trained with observational data be turned into counterfactual world models and support effective policy learning through RLB? Details can be found in Appendix C, and supplementary results can be found in Appendix D. 5.1 CONTEXTUAL BANDIT We first study the benefits of counterfactuals in setting where the optimal policy is known. 8 Preprint. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We studied counterfactual world models, which predict how observations would change under alternative actions. REINFORCE Look Back (RLB) uses their predicted returns as baselines to separate action effects from environmental luck. It is unbiased under exact counterfactuals, has bias bounded by the model error otherwise, and can reduce variance when environmental noise dominates. When action effects are more predictable than the environment, counterfactual world models are easier to learn and yield better policies than ordinary ones. Future work includes larger diffusion models and connecting to GRPO-style methods. Our results suggest that agents in big worlds may learn by looking back at what happened, without modeling the full complexity of their environments. 11 Preprint.

sections.title: B EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: In this section, we provide an extended discussion of related work across domains. Policy gradients with grouped baselines. RLB constructs learning signals by comparing multiple samples associated with common input. Its parent method, RLOO (Kool et al., 2019; Ahmadian et al., 2024) uses the mean return of other independently sampled trajectories as leave-one-out baseline. Relatedly, GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) normalizes rewards within groups of responses to the same prompt for clipped policy updates. Yet, sharing starting state or prompt does not itself couple environmental randomness. We adapt RLOO baseline but generate counterfactual branches conditioned on factual. Given the close relationship between RLOO and GRPO (Lan, 2026), we conjecture that our approach could be extended to GRPO, which we leave as future work. Policy gradients with shared randomness. Our work is closely related with prior work that leverages common random numbers to reduce the variance of policy gradient estimators. TRPOs vine procedure (Schulman et al., 2015) compares actions through rollouts using common random numbers and requires simulator resets to sampled states. Input-dependent baselines (Mao et al., 2018) condition value predictions on observed future exogenous inputs. Hindsight learning (Sinclair et al., 2023) uses logged exogenous inputs and known dynamics to evaluate actions through hindsight planning. Exogenous-state methods remove exogenous state variables and rewards when the reward decomposes additively (Dietterich et al., 2018), or learn with sample complexity that is nearly independent of an unknown exogenous part of the state that does not affect rewards (Efroni et al., 31 Preprint. 2022). rMC (Bazerghi et al., 2025) estimates policy gradients for finite MDPs from return differences between root trajectory and coupled true counterfactuals for all alternative actions run until they merge with the root. We employ learned counterfactual dynamics, allowing policy learning without online simulator resets or direct online observation of environmental noise. Exogenous inputs and states. Among the policy gradient methods above, those that use exogenous inputs or states are the closest to ours. They are given the noise, as inputs (Mao et al., 2018; Sinclair et al., 2023) or as part of the state (Dietterich et al., 2018; Efroni et al., 2022), whereas RLB only needs the factual observations, from which CWM predicts the counterfactual transitions. The noise thus need not be separate input or part of the state, nor behave additively. If the noise is given as an input sequence, the baseline of RLB is Monte Carlo estimate of the input-dependent baseline of Mao et al. (2018). If the reward decomposes additively as in Dietterich et al. (2018), RLB removes the exogenous return without discovering the decomposition. In Efroni et al. (2022), the exogenous part of the state does not affect rewards and is to be ignored, whereas the noise that we consider affects returns. Hindsight learning (Sinclair et al., 2023) assumes known dynamics and lets planner see the future inputs, which biases its values towards foresight, whereas the policy of RLB does not see the future noise, so its gradient is unbiased as long as CWM is exact. Hindsight and counterfactual credit assignment. Prior work has used hindsight and counterfactual predictions to distinguish action effects from luck. HCA (Harutyunyan et al., 2019) assigns credit using action probabilities conditioned on future observations. CCA (Mesnard et al., 2020a) learns value baselines from hindsight features, encouraging independence from current action. QCA (Mesnard et al., 2023) compares return distributions at the quantile level and predicts it from future observations. COMA (Foerster et al., 2018) uses centralized critic to marginalize one agents action while fixing the others, and its baseline follows difference rewards (Wolpert & Tumer, 2002). In our multi-agent bandit, where the other agents are the environmental noise of an agent, RLB is sampled version of this baseline, and the learned CWM computes it from each agents own observation without centralized critic. We build baselines from generated counterfactual trajectories, without separate critic that predicts returns, coupling transition outcomes through factual observations instead of e.g. return quantiles. We note that an older preprint of CCA (Mesnard et al., 2020b) has theorized vine extension motivated by that of TRPO in Appendix E.2, and separately theorized model extension in Appendix E.3 (see also Corollary 1 in the latest version), yet the precise combination of leave-one-out baseline with counterfactual models as in our work has not been considered, and their implemented methods are all model-free and use learned value baselines. Counterfactual inference for policy search and evaluation. Similar to our CWMs, prior work has used observed experience to improve simulations of alternative decisions. Abbeel et al. (2006) correct approximate dynamics using real trajectories for local policy improvement in nearly deterministic settings. CF-GPS (Buesing et al., 2018) infers scenarios from logged episodes, simulates It motivates facalternative policies, and improves policies through return-weighted regression. tual conditioning when scenario distributions are harder to model than causal mechanisms, thereby inspiring our approach. Oberst & Sontag (2019) reuse inferred Gumbel noise under alternative policies for counterfactual off-policy evaluation. Distinguished from these approaches, we employ grouped policy gradient estimator using learned counterfactual transitions, where both the factual and counterfactual contribute to each update. In addition, CF-GPS is given the mechanisms and infers only the noise of logged episode, whereas CWM learns the counterfactual transition itself. Identifiability of counterfactuals. The transitions of an MDP do not identify its counterfactuals, as SCMs with the same transitions can disagree on them (Oberst & Sontag, 2019). Prior work is therefore given the noise or the mechanisms (Mao et al., 2018; Sinclair et al., 2023; Buesing et al., 2018), or restricts the mechanisms such that the transitions determine the counterfactuals, e.g., to Gumbel-max mechanisms (Oberst & Sontag, 2019). RLB needs neither, as it uses counterfactuals only as means to estimate the policy gradient, for which every SCM consistent with the MDP gives an unbiased estimate and the choice among them only affects the variance (Corollary 1). Learned and generative counterfactual inference. Our approach is related to, and can benefit from, methods for inferring and learning counterfactual dynamics. CoPhy (Baradel et al., 2019) prePreprint. dicts physical trajectories under altered initial conditions from factual experience, using paired factual and counterfactual training data similarly to our CWMs. Filtered-CoPhy (Janny et al., 2022) extends this to video prediction without object position or physical property supervision, using paired videos. We study similar prediction problem in action-conditioned prediction setting, and further study modeling difficulty depending on environmental properties. Diff-SCM (Sanchez & Tsaftaris, 2022) and DCM (Chao et al., 2023) use diffusion-based latent inference to generate counterfactuals in class-conditional image generation and medical application, respectively. CWMDT (Shen et al., 2025) conditions video diffusion on scene descriptions modified by language model. Distinctly, we apply diffusion counterfactual inference to an action-conditioned WM trained on interaction data. Advantage functions. The weight G(j) b(j) that RLB gives to trajectory estimates (u), the return of the trajectory relative to the expected return of the policy under the same environmental noise. It differs from the usual advantage, which is relative to the expected return over all noise, by the luck (u) E[V (u)], which state-dependent baseline cannot remove (Lemma 9). This hindsight advantage is targeted by input-dependent baselines (Mao et al., 2018) and future-conditional value functions (Mesnard et al., 2020a) with learned critic, whereas RLB estimates it in criticfree manner. If part of the noise is hidden, the baseline estimates E[V (u)ˆτ ] instead, which is posterior value function (Nota et al., 2021) with the noise as the hidden variable.

sections.title: D SUPPLEMENTARY RESULTS
sections.content: We present supplementary results we could not include in the main text due to space limits. D.1 ANALYSIS OF BIAS AND VARIANCE We empirically analyze the bias and variance of the policy gradient estimators, in particular RLOO and RLB under the use of learned (counterfactual) world models. Contextual bandit. We compare all methods in the contextual bandit of Section 5.1 in terms of variance and size of the bias relative to that of the gradient. We fix the same uniform policy and use the same budget of 256 transitions per batch across all methods, using five seeds. Because the true policy gradient can be computed exactly in this environment, the bias can be measured directly. The results are in Table 3. With almost zero environmental noise (σ = 0.1), RLB and RLOO have the same variance, because there is little noise to share. As the noise grows, RLB has the lowest variance of all methods, 1214 lower than RLOO and REINFORCE at σ = 30, and 4550 lower at σ = 60. RLB + CWM keeps this reduction, while RLOO + WM does not, presumably due to the difficulty of learning the WM (Section 5.1). CCA and RLOO + WM are biased, and their bias grows with the noise, whereas RLB + CWM is empirically nearly unbiased (relative bias 0.003). We further measure the bias of RLB + CWM during CWM training, at the final RLB + CWM policy rather than the uniform policy of Table 3. At σ = 30, the relative bias is 1.0 at initialization, briefly rises to 1.43 for an intermediate model, and falls to 0.0025 for the fully trained CWM. The result shows that, as CWM becomes more accurate through training, it reduces the bias of policy gradient estimation, consistent with our Propositions 10 and 11. Dino. While exact diffusion inversion would recover latent noise independent of the action underlying the factual (Section 3.1), and therefore yield unbiased policy gradient estimate in RLB (Proposition 8), diffusion inversion is not exact in practice, which means the information of the action can leak into the baseline and introduce bias (Proposition 10). To test if this happens in practice, we train small nonlinear action classifier to predict the factual action from the inverted noise, and also the generated counterfactual. By training an action classifier on the inverted noise using 600 training data, 300 validation data, and 3,000 unseen test data, we find that the factual action is recoverable with 98% test accuracy, whereas the chance level is 33%. Thus, the inverted latent does retain substantial information about the factual action. While this may appear as inducing substantial bias in RLB, we remark that what matters for the bias is whether this information reaches the counterfactual branches, as Propositions 10 and 11 predict that the bias is bounded by the error of counterfactuals and their returns. Therefore, we additionally train the same classifier to predict the factual action from generated counterfactuals. For the same data, we draw new action uniformly from three choices and generate the counterfactual from the inverted noise with this action. We then give the classifier the counterfactual, the last context frame, and the new action. Its test accuracy is 53.4% 0.8% over five seeds, no higher than the 54.8% 0.6% of classifier that sees only the context frame and the new action2. Thus, the classifier detects no information of factual action in the generated counterfactual beyond the context and new action, consistent with the small overall bias of RLB + CWM measured in Appendix D.1.
